steps.prompt: Without working it out: is $1234 \times 5678$ odd or even, and what is its last digit? How could that help on a multiple-choice question?
steps.placeholder: It is… Its last digit is… It helps because…

cards.title: Estimate first
cards.body: Round the numbers and work out roughly what the answer must be. Choices far from your estimate are out. Often only one choice survives, and you never needed the exact value.

steps.text: Only (C) is near $1000$. The nearest other choices are twice as big or half as big, so the rounding can't change the answer.

cards.title: Eliminate with quick checks
cards.body: You can rule out choices without solving: check the last digit, odd or even, the sign, and the size. If the answer must be a multiple of $3$, cross out the choices that aren't. Each choice you rule out also makes a guess worth more.

steps.text: Last digits: $7 \times 3 = 21$ ends in $1$ and $5 \times 2 = 10$ ends in $0$, so the answer ends in $1$. That rules out (A) and (C).
Size: $27 \times 43$ is about $30 \times 40 = 1200$ and $15 \times 12 = 180$, so the answer is near $1300$–$1400$. That rules out (E).

cards.title: The common trap: estimating close choices
cards.body: An estimate can't split two choices that are close together. When two choices are both near your estimate, stop rounding: work it out exactly, or use a check like the last digit to split them.

prompts: Which quick check (size, last digit, odd or even) will you try first on a test, and why?
